segments.narration: Every queue is a small government. It has a constitution, usually unwritten: one person, one place; no proxies after a certain hour; the elderly and the pregnant may be waved forward by common consent.
segments.anchor: Every queue is a small government. It has a constitution, usually unwritten: one person, one place; no proxies after a certain hour; the elderly and the pregnant may be waved forward by common consent.

segments.narration: It has enforcement — the cough, the stare, the muttered escalation — and it has diplomacy, the negotiated absence: "I'm just going to move my car, this is my spot."
segments.anchor: It has enforcement — the cough, the stare, the muttered escalation — and it has diplomacy, the negotiated absence ("I'm just going to move my car, this is my spot").

segments.narration: It has, above all, a theory of fairness so widely shared that no one thinks of it as a theory at all.
segments.anchor: It has, above all, a theory of fairness so widely shared that no one thinks of it as a theory at all.

segments.narration: This is why queue-jumping enrages out of all proportion to its cost. Thirty seconds of delay would be forgiven from a slow cashier without a second thought.
segments.anchor: This is why queue-jumping enrages out of all proportion to its cost. Thirty seconds of delay would be forgiven from a slow cashier without a second thought.

segments.narration: The same thirty seconds, taken by a man sliding in near the front, feels like an act of violence — because it is not a theft of time but a repudiation of the constitution.
segments.anchor: The same thirty seconds, taken by a man sliding in near the front, feels like an act of violence — because it is not a theft of time but a repudiation of the constitution.

segments.narration: He has declared, in front of everyone, that the government does not exist for him.
segments.anchor: He has declared, in front of everyone, that the government does not exist for him.

segments.narration: Every queue member feels the insult personally, because each of them has been paying taxes to that government since they arrived: standing when they could have pushed, waiting when they could have schemed.
segments.anchor: Every queue member feels the insult personally, because each of them has been paying taxes to that government since they arrived: standing when they could have pushed, waiting when they could have schemed.

segments.narration: Notice, too, how quickly the state forms. Three people at a bus stop are a crowd; four are a queue, and the fourth arrival can usually reconstruct the order of the first three without asking.
segments.anchor: Notice, too, how quickly the state forms. Three people at a bus stop are a crowd; four are a queue, and the fourth arrival can usually reconstruct the order of the first three without asking.

segments.narration: We assemble these micro-nations dozens of times a day, ratify their laws by standing still, and dissolve them without ceremony the moment the bus arrives.
segments.anchor: We assemble these micro-nations dozens of times a day, ratify their laws by standing still, and dissolve them without ceremony the moment the bus arrives.

segments.narration: No flags, no anthems, and yet I have seen men in expensive suits — men who negotiate for a living and would call patriotism sentimental — go visibly red defending the sovereignty of a sandwich line.
segments.anchor: No flags, no anthems, and yet I have seen men in expensive suits — men who negotiate for a living and would call patriotism sentimental — go visibly red defending the sovereignty of a sandwich line.

segments.narration: The queue is proof of something we rarely credit ourselves with: that ordinary people, unsupervised, will build fairness out of nothing but shared standing and mutual watching, and will pay real costs to maintain it.
segments.anchor: The queue is proof of something we rarely credit ourselves with: that ordinary people, unsupervised, will build fairness out of nothing but shared standing and mutual watching, and will pay real costs to maintain it.

segments.narration: It is also proof of the fragility underneath. One unpunished violation and the constitution wobbles; two, and men who waited politely for twenty minutes begin edging forward, because no one keeps paying taxes to a government that has stopped existing.

segments.narration: Order of this kind is not a possession. It is a practice, renewed by every person who joins the end of the line when no one would have stopped them doing otherwise.
